name: Design a URL Shortener
description: Design a URL shortening service like bit.ly that can handle millions of URLs.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a URL shortening service that takes long URLs and creates short aliases. When users visit the short URL, they should be redirected to the original.
requirements: Generate unique short URLs from long URLs
Redirect short URLs to original URLs with low latency
constraints: Short URL should be at most 7 characters
evaluationCriteria: Hash/encoding strategy for short URL generation
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Use Base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing counter (distributed via Zookeeper ranges). Store mappings in a sharded NoSQL database (key: shortUrl, value: longUrl). Add a Redis cache layer for hot URLs. Use Kafka for async analytics event processing. CDN for global low-latency redirects.

name: Design a Rate Limiter
description: Understand the tradeoffs between different rate limiting algorithms.

mcqOptions.text: Fixed window counter resets at fixed intervals and can allow 2x the rate at window boundaries
mcqOptions.explanation: Fixed window counters reset at interval boundaries. A burst at the end of one window and start of the next can allow double the intended rate.

mcqOptions.text: Token bucket cannot handle burst traffic
mcqOptions.explanation: Token bucket explicitly supports burst traffic — tokens accumulate up to a max bucket size, allowing short bursts.

mcqOptions.text: Sliding window log is the most memory-efficient algorithm
mcqOptions.explanation: Sliding window log stores every request timestamp, making it the LEAST memory-efficient. Sliding window counter is more efficient.

mcqOptions.text: Leaky bucket processes requests at a variable rate
mcqOptions.explanation: Leaky bucket processes requests at a FIXED rate regardless of input rate, smoothing out bursts.

name: Design a Chat System
description: Design a real-time chat system supporting 1:1 and group messaging.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a chat application like WhatsApp or Slack that supports real-time messaging between users.
constraints: Messages delivered in < 500ms for online users
evaluationCriteria: WebSocket vs long polling for real-time delivery
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: WebSocket connections through a gateway service. Message queue (Kafka) for reliable delivery. Chat service writes to a message store (Cassandra for write-heavy workload). Fan-out-on-write for small groups, fan-out-on-read for large channels. Presence service using heartbeats with Redis. Push notifications via FCM/APNs for offline users.

name: CAP Theorem
description: Understand the CAP theorem and its implications for distributed databases.

mcqOptions.text: A system can guarantee all three: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
mcqOptions.explanation: The CAP theorem proves that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot guarantee all three simultaneously.

mcqOptions.text: During a network partition, a CP system sacrifices availability to maintain consistency
mcqOptions.explanation: CP systems (like HBase, MongoDB) refuse to serve requests during partitions rather than risk returning stale data, sacrificing availability for consistency.

mcqOptions.text: AP systems never return stale data
mcqOptions.explanation: AP systems (like Cassandra, DynamoDB) prioritize availability during partitions and may return stale data, achieving eventual consistency.

mcqOptions.text: The CAP theorem only applies to SQL databases
mcqOptions.explanation: CAP applies to ALL distributed data stores regardless of data model — SQL, NoSQL, key-value, document, etc.

name: Design a Key-Value Store
description: Design a distributed key-value store like DynamoDB or Redis Cluster.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a distributed key-value store that supports put(key, value) and get(key) operations with high availability.
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes for even distribution. N=3 replicas with configurable W and R quorum. Vector clocks for conflict detection, application-level resolution. Gossip protocol for membership and failure detection. Merkle trees per partition for background sync. Hinted handoff for temporary failures.

name: Database Indexing Strategies
description: Understand when and how to use database indexes effectively.

mcqOptions.text: Adding more indexes always improves query performance
mcqOptions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes — every INSERT/UPDATE must also update all indexes. Over-indexing can degrade overall performance.

mcqOptions.text: A compound index on (A, B) can satisfy queries filtering on A alone but not B alone
mcqOptions.explanation: Compound indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule. An index on (A, B) can serve queries on A or (A, B), but not B alone — B is only sorted within each A value.

mcqOptions.text: B-tree indexes are ideal for full-text search
mcqOptions.explanation: B-tree indexes are optimized for equality and range queries. Full-text search requires inverted indexes (like those in Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL's GIN indexes).

mcqOptions.text: Covering indexes are indexes that span all tables in a database
mcqOptions.explanation: A covering index includes all columns needed by a query, allowing the database to serve the query entirely from the index without accessing the table (index-only scan).

name: Design a REST API
description: Understand REST API design principles and best practices.

mcqOptions.text: REST APIs should use verbs in URL paths (e.g., /getUsers, /deletePost)
mcqOptions.explanation: REST uses nouns for resources (/users, /posts) and HTTP methods (GET, DELETE) for actions. Verbs in URLs is an anti-pattern.

mcqOptions.text: Idempotency means calling an operation multiple times produces the same result as calling it once
mcqOptions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE should be idempotent. POST is typically not idempotent. Idempotency is crucial for retry safety in distributed systems.

mcqOptions.text: HTTP 200 is the correct status code for a successful resource creation
mcqOptions.explanation: 201 Created is the correct status for successful resource creation. 200 OK is for successful retrieval or update operations.

mcqOptions.text: GraphQL is a type of REST API
mcqOptions.explanation: GraphQL is a distinct query language and runtime — it uses a single endpoint with POST requests, while REST uses multiple endpoints with HTTP methods.

name: Design an API Rate Limiting Service
description: Design a centralized rate limiting service for a microservices architecture.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a rate limiting service that multiple backend services can use to enforce per-user and per-API rate limits.
requirements: Support multiple rate limiting algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket)
Per-user, per-API, and global rate limits
Graceful degradation when rate limiter is unavailable
constraints: No false negatives (never allow over-limit requests)
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Redis-backed with Lua scripts for atomic operations. Sliding window counter as default algorithm. Client library with local token bucket as first-line defense, Redis check as second line. Rules stored in Redis with pub/sub for hot reload. If Redis unavailable, fall back to local rate limiting with conservative limits. Return rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-*) for client visibility.

name: Caching Strategies
description: Understand different caching strategies and their tradeoffs.

mcqOptions.text: Write-through cache has higher write latency but ensures cache consistency
mcqOptions.explanation: Write-through writes to both cache and database synchronously. Higher write latency (two writes) but cache always has latest data. Good for read-heavy workloads where consistency matters.

mcqOptions.text: Cache-aside (lazy loading) prevents cache stampede by default
mcqOptions.explanation: Cache-aside is vulnerable to cache stampede — when a popular key expires, many requests simultaneously hit the database. Stampede protection (mutex locks, probabilistic early expiry) must be added explicitly.

mcqOptions.text: Write-behind cache guarantees zero data loss
mcqOptions.explanation: Write-behind (write-back) buffers writes and flushes asynchronously. If the cache node crashes before flushing, buffered writes are lost. It trades durability for write performance.

mcqOptions.text: TTL-based expiry is the only way to invalidate cached data
mcqOptions.explanation: Other strategies include explicit invalidation (delete on write), event-driven invalidation (pub/sub), and versioned keys. TTL is the simplest but can serve stale data.

name: Design a CDN
description: Design a Content Delivery Network for global content distribution.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a CDN that distributes static and dynamic content to users worldwide with minimal latency.
requirements: Support for static files, streaming, and dynamic content
Real-time analytics on cache hit rates and latency
constraints: Cache hit ratio > 95% for static content
First byte time < 50ms for cached content
evaluationCriteria: Cache key design and vary headers
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Two-tier cache hierarchy: edge PoPs in major cities + regional aggregation nodes. Anycast DNS for routing to nearest PoP. Consistent hashing within each PoP for cache distribution. Origin shield as a reverse proxy cache before the origin. Cache keys include URL + relevant Vary headers. Purge via fan-out from control plane to all PoPs. Tiered TTLs: immutable assets (1 year), API responses (configurable). Streaming via chunked transfer with edge buffering.

name: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
description: Understand when to scale horizontally vs vertically.

mcqOptions.text: Vertical scaling requires application code changes
mcqOptions.explanation: Vertical scaling (adding more CPU/RAM to existing server) typically requires NO code changes — the application runs on the same machine with more resources.

mcqOptions.text: Horizontal scaling adds complexity around data consistency and session management
mcqOptions.explanation: With multiple servers, you need load balancing, sticky sessions or externalized session stores, distributed caching, and strategies for data consistency across nodes.

mcqOptions.text: Vertical scaling has no upper limit
mcqOptions.explanation: Vertical scaling is bounded by the maximum hardware available — there's a ceiling on how much CPU/RAM a single machine can have.

mcqOptions.text: Horizontal scaling is always cheaper than vertical scaling
mcqOptions.explanation: For small to medium workloads, a single larger server can be cheaper than managing multiple smaller ones (no load balancer, simpler ops). Horizontal becomes cost-effective at scale.

name: Design a Load Balancer
description: Design a Layer 7 load balancer for a web application.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a load balancer that distributes HTTP traffic across backend servers with health checking and session affinity.
requirements: Multiple load balancing algorithms (round robin, least connections, weighted)
Health checking with automatic server removal/addition
Request rate limiting per client IP
constraints: Add/remove backend servers with zero downtime
No single point of failure for the load balancer itself
evaluationCriteria: L4 vs L7 load balancing tradeoffs
High availability of the load balancer itself
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: L7 reverse proxy (like Nginx/HAProxy). Active health checks every 5s + passive monitoring of response errors. Consistent hashing on session cookie for affinity (falls back to round-robin for new sessions). SSL termination at LB with certificate management. HA via active-passive pair with VRRP/keepalived. Connection draining: stop sending new requests to removed server, wait for in-flight to complete (30s timeout). Rate limiting via token bucket per client IP in shared memory.

name: Consistent Hashing
description: Understand consistent hashing and its use in distributed systems.

mcqOptions.text: When a node is added to a consistent hash ring, all keys must be redistributed
mcqOptions.explanation: Only keys in the range between the new node and its predecessor need to move — on average K/N keys (where K is total keys, N is total nodes). This is the key advantage over simple modular hashing.

mcqOptions.text: Virtual nodes help solve the problem of uneven key distribution across physical nodes
mcqOptions.explanation: Without virtual nodes, nodes may be unevenly spaced on the ring, causing hot spots. Virtual nodes (multiple points per physical node) ensure more uniform distribution — each physical node owns many small ranges instead of one large one.

mcqOptions.text: Consistent hashing guarantees perfectly equal load distribution
mcqOptions.explanation: Even with virtual nodes, consistent hashing only provides approximately equal distribution. Perfect equality would require dynamic rebalancing based on actual load, not just key count.

mcqOptions.text: Consistent hashing is only used for cache distribution
mcqOptions.explanation: Consistent hashing is used in many distributed systems: database sharding (DynamoDB, Cassandra), load balancing, distributed caches, CDNs, and distributed file systems.

name: Design a Notification System
description: Design a scalable notification system supporting push, SMS, and email.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a notification system that can send push notifications, SMS, and emails to millions of users.
requirements: Support multiple channels: push (iOS/Android), SMS, email
User notification preferences (opt-in/out per channel and type)
constraints: Rate limiting per user (max 5 notifications per hour)
evaluationCriteria: Third-party service integration (APNs, FCM, Twilio, SendGrid)
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Event-driven architecture with Kafka as the message backbone. Notification service receives events, resolves user preferences, and fans out to channel-specific queues. Each channel has dedicated workers with provider SDKs. Priority queue (separate Kafka topic) for urgent notifications. Template service with variable substitution. Redis for rate limiting and de-duplication (message ID tracking). DLQ for failed deliveries with exponential backoff retry. Analytics via event streaming to data warehouse.

name: SQL vs NoSQL
description: Understand when to choose SQL vs NoSQL databases.

mcqOptions.text: NoSQL databases cannot perform joins
mcqOptions.explanation: Some NoSQL databases support joins (MongoDB $lookup, Couchbase N1QL). The distinction is that NoSQL databases typically don't enforce referential integrity and denormalization is preferred over joins for performance.

mcqOptions.text: SQL databases are better suited when you need ACID transactions across multiple entities
mcqOptions.explanation: SQL databases provide native ACID transactions across tables. While some NoSQL databases support transactions (MongoDB multi-document), SQL databases are purpose-built for complex transactional workloads with referential integrity.

mcqOptions.text: NoSQL databases are always faster than SQL databases
mcqOptions.explanation: Speed depends on access patterns. SQL with proper indexes can outperform NoSQL for complex queries with joins. NoSQL excels at simple key-value lookups and document retrieval at scale.

mcqOptions.text: You should always start with NoSQL for new projects
mcqOptions.explanation: SQL is often the better default — it provides flexibility for evolving schemas, built-in data integrity, and powerful querying. Choose NoSQL when you have specific needs: massive scale, flexible schema, or access patterns that don't fit relational models.

name: Design a Search Autocomplete System
description: Design a real-time search autocomplete/typeahead system.

designPrompt.scenario: Design a typeahead suggestion system that shows top search suggestions as users type, similar to Google Search autocomplete.
requirements: Return top 5 suggestions within 100ms of each keystroke
Support personalized suggestions based on user history
Update suggestion rankings as search trends change
constraints: Suggestions must be safe (no offensive content)
evaluationCriteria: Trie vs inverted index for prefix matching
designPrompt.sampleAnswer: Trie data structure with frequency counts at each node. Top-K results cached at each prefix node. Two-tier architecture: real-time trie in Redis for hot queries, batch-rebuilt trie from Hadoop/Spark for comprehensive coverage. Zookeeper for trie version management across replicas. Sampling collector aggregates search queries into frequency counts hourly. Content filter service screens suggestions before indexing. Client-side debounce (200ms) + browser caching of recent prefixes.
